I don't have much to say from a code perspective. I also think a better experience when exporting non-nullable reference types would be a good addition to Godot. However, I have a few reservations.

There might have been a discussion to be had about this new validation being either "throw" or "set a default value" depending on the type. I'm not sure that it feels right. I'm also unsure if throwing an error to the console is the best user feedback for this. That's why this should probably have gone through a proposal (and I know, we haven't especially been on top of the `topic:dotnet` proposals, sorry).

I'm also weary about introducing something that is likely to regress as soon as godot-dotnet hits the road.

As a last point, I'm not sure about the implications of creating a new notification. I imagine as a rule of thumb, we want to keep the notification count as low as possible, but I'll let someone with better core knowledge correct me on this.

> I'm also unsure if throwing an error to the console is the best user feedback for this.

The reason this PR raises an exception is that it is common practice in C#. When something goes wrong, if the user is running the Game in an IDE with a Debugger, it will automatically suspend execution. The `ArgumentNullException` choice provides a clearer error message to hint to the user that they might have forgotten to assign these variables in the inspector.

> That's why this should probably have gone through a proposal

I can definitely write one if the team would like to gather more feedback before proceeding. Our team has already been using this feature in production (in our fork), and it significantly reduces the mental burden by eliminating over 1,000 lines of unnecessary not-null assertions. Additionally, it already reveals some of our unassigned parameters, reducing unnecessary testing overhead (in case we start using these variables in the future). Since these null checks are performed during instantiation rather than when accessing the variable, they provide a more accurate assessment.

> I'm also weary about introducing something that is likely to regress as soon as godot-dotnet hits the road.

I can start researching to port this feature to `godot-dotnet`. I believe the requirement for nullability support isn't explicitly tied to the mono module, especially now that we are also introducing [nullability annotations to the APIs](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/86079).

> I'm not sure about the implications of creating a new notification. I imagine as a rule of thumb, we want to keep the notification count as low as possible, but I'll let someone with better core knowledge correct me on this.

I would totally welcome an alternate solution if there is one. The notification approach is a last resort, as I can't find a suitable execution point to invoke the generated C# check method (after all the exported properties have been assigned and before any other notification), similar to `NOTIFICATION_PREDELETE_CLEANUP` I saw in the version history that the team uses internally, this notification is not bound and should be an internal implementation detail.

I wonder, doesn't the compiler enforce these non-null fields to be initialized inline or in the constructor? How does this PR deal with that?

I too have doubts about throwing here being correct. What happens to the object/node? Does it remain alive in an invalid state?

I think this should be handled by Godot itself, and this would benefit other languages other than C# (and GDScript if it ever adds non-nullables). It could be something like this:

- Any live editor (like the SceneTree) should not construct the object/node until all its non-null properties are assigned a non-null value. It could use a placeholder meanwhile (although the user should see the normal type).
- An error should be displayed for the object/node, similar to how it's done when a physics body is missing a collision shape.
- The object/node should still be saved/serialized even if it has an invalid state.
- The deserializer (be it PackedScene, resource loaders, or whatever else) should refuse to construct the object (and its children) if any of its non-null properties are missing a non-null value.

Of course, that's much more work, but I think it's worth it. It's missing how to deal with instantiations from code. Perhaps by disabling parameterless construction?

> I too have doubts about throwing here being correct. What happens to the object/node? Does it remain alive in an invalid state?

I'm here using an exception as it's easy to be catched by debugger, and I do think this is the correct C# approach. The target object/node will be in an valid state with the corresponding field remains null if the exceptions are not caught by the debugger.

With a big prerequisite: Runtime Only. In our production project we found throwing expection in editor environement is really annoying when dealing with [Tool] scripts, that's why [[1cd4fb8](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/112195/commits/1cd4fb8fe127d6d81caa7a5cd6538135212be682)] changed the PR to only create godot error under editor environemnt.

> I think this should be handled by Godot itself, and this would benefit other languages other than C# (and GDScript if it ever adds non-nullables). It could be something like this:

I generally agrees, but I think these should mostly a runtime guard instead of edit time guard:

> - Any live editor (like the SceneTree) should not construct the object/node until all its non-null properties are assigned a non-null value. It could use a placeholder meanwhile (although the user should see the normal type).

We should allow constructions of these types in editor, and throws error in runtime, that follows the typical Godot editing experiences, only with additional errors when the Godot is trying to load the target packed scene or resource.

> - An error should be displayed for the object/node, similar to how it's done when a physics body is missing a collision shape.

Yes, as an editor side warning of not-nullable fields are left empty, which will causes error in runtime.

> - The object/node should still be saved/serialized even if it has an invalid state.

Yes, so the exisiting code works and the developer can still open the resource or scene to fix these unassigned errors.

> - The deserializer (be it PackedScene, resource loaders, or whatever else) should refuse to construct the object (and its children) if any of its non-null properties are missing a non-null value.

Yes.

The overall goal of this PR is to implemnt most of these on the C# binding level so it only touches the scope I familier, adding nullability to Godot Scripting world is a very large thing and is most likely be rejected by the GDScript team, but It's a common C# conecpt (since C# 8, and now we are at C# 14), plus I do need this feature to guard our large production project, that's why it's only C# scoped. C# thing, done in C# bindnig layer.

> Of course, that's much more work, but I think it's worth it. It's missing how to deal with instantiations from code. Perhaps by disabling parameterless construction?

I think most of these are already finished at C# level by this PR, parameterless constructions are guarenteed to cause C# exceptions, so if the developer wants to instantiate these checked hybrid type by code, they have to implement both a parametered ctor for C# instantiation and a parameterless ctor for runtime instantitaion. That can also be guareded by a dedicated analyzer.

Sorry for grammar mistakes or typo, I don't have my grammar checker on this device.

All right, I'm that much against the throwing way, but there is one big thing that I don't like.
It seems this relies on a pattern of lying to the compiler about the nullability of these fields. Non-nullables are meant to be non-null always and everywhere, but this PR asserts these fields will be null after construction (and thus within the constructors) until Godot actually assigns the properties. **EDIT: Did I understand this correctly or is this not how this PR works?**
This is probably unsolvable unless Godot were to pass the initial values of the properties to the constructor. If that cannot be done, perhaps this PR could still be considered a valid workaround, but it irks me the wrong way.

> we instead guarentees the compiler that, when the life time of any of these fields are active, they will be in a not-null state, the only difference is that we have an additional initialization step before these fields enter their life time scope.

But are we correctly guaranteeing that actually? The life time of those fields is active during the constructor call. If the constructor tries to use the field, what will happen? Compiler warning/error or runtime NullReferenceException? I assume the latter, because how can we even determined some other method that accesses the field is not being called from the constructor?

I don't know how Unity serialization works. Their construction order might is different from Godot's.

> The life time of those fields is active during the constructor call. If the constructor tries to use the field, what will happen? Compiler warning/error or runtime NullReferenceException? I assume the latter, because how can we even determined some other method that accesses the field is not being called from the constructor? This PR already gracefully handles that; when accessing these exported fields in the constructor without initializing them, they are treated as maybe null by default. I already encountered this exact issue you mentioned when using a prior version of this PR in production and have already patched it. > However, if you initialize the StrField after the call to MethodThatAccessesStrField(), you get no warning, despite that method accessing the field. This results in a NullReferenceException at runtime without any compiler warning. This is a limitation in the C# compiler's flow analysis. There isn't much we can do about this in this PR. But writing custom ctors for hybrid types is already rare in Godot (we initialize in _Ready), let alone calling methods in a ctor. So yes, we are doing kind of best-effort delivery rather than strong guarentee in this PR.

> Regarding Unity, do they actually guarantee that the fields will be initialized with a non-null value, or do they need validity checks like this PR?

It's been a while since I opened my last unity product, but I do remember they throw MissingReferenceException on callsites?
